lessons.title: Play-Action, Boots and Screens
lessons.blurb: Using the run to set up the pass.

steps.title: Play-action
steps.body: The quarterback fakes a handoff. Linebackers and safeties step up for the run, and receivers get behind them.

steps.title: Boot
steps.body: After the run fake one way, the quarterback rolls out the other way, usually with a tight end crossing toward him and receivers flooding that side at different depths.

steps.title: The screen game
steps.body: A running back slip screen, a wide receiver bubble or tunnel, a middle screen: each lets the rush come or the defense drop, then throws short behind blockers.

steps.prompt: Why does play-action work best when the run game is working?
choices: Defenders respect the fake and step up
The clock keeps running during the fake
The quarterback gets a longer drop
steps.explanation: The more a defense fears the run, the harder it bites on the fake.

steps.statement: On a bootleg, the quarterback rolls out the same way as the run fake.
steps.explanation: On a bootleg the quarterback fakes the run one way and rolls out the other.

lessons.title: College Game Day
lessons.blurb: Option, tempo, pressure and the red zone.

steps.title: Make the call
steps.body: Each card is a game moment. Pick the call most modern coaches and win-probability models would make, then see why.

steps.prompt: 1st and goal at the 1, second quarter, tied. What's the call?

options.why: One yard is the shortest, highest-percentage play in football.
Pressure and a sack lose yards you can't afford.
Gives up three downs to score seven.

steps.explanation: Short yardage at the goal line: run it in.

steps.prompt: The defense subs into dime on 2nd and 3. What do you call?

options.why: Six defensive backs means a light box: run at it.
Reasonable, but the run is the clear advantage.
Dime is built to stop exactly that.

steps.explanation: Attack the personnel the defense chose.

steps.prompt: 3rd and 8. Two linebackers walk up into the A gaps. What's your adjustment?

options.text: Set the protection to the A gaps and have a quick throw ready
options.why: ID the threat, block the middle, and know where the hot throw goes.

options.text: Seven-step drop for a deep shot
options.why: Interior pressure arrives before a deep route can open.
Unblocked A-gap rushers mean a sack.

steps.explanation: Name the threat before the snap.

steps.prompt: Zone read. The unblocked end crashes down hard on the back. Give or keep?

options.why: He took the back, so the edge is open for the quarterback.
Handing off into a crashing end is exactly what he wants.
There's a free run available.

steps.prompt: RPO: the nickel steps into the box at the snap. Hand off or throw the bubble?

options.why: With the nickel in the box, the slot is uncovered.
You'd run into the extra defender.
Possible, but the bubble is the designed answer.

steps.explanation: The conflict defender tells you where the ball goes.

steps.prompt: 50 seconds left in the half. You just completed a pass in bounds at your 35; the clock is running. What now?

options.text: Hurry to the line and snap
options.why: No-huddle saves the most time and keeps your timeouts.
Stops the clock, but costs a timeout you might need later.
A huddle burns precious seconds.

steps.explanation: In the two-minute drill, tempo is a timeout you don't have to spend.

steps.prompt: 4th and 2 at their 38, down 4 in the third quarter. What's the call?

options.why: A 55-yard field goal is a low-percentage kick, and two yards converts often.
Pins them deep but gives up a good chance to keep the drive.
55 yards is a long shot that also hands them good field position if it misses.

steps.explanation: In no-man's-land, short yardage usually means go.

steps.prompt: 3rd and 5. No safety deep and everyone walked up: it looks like Cover 0. What do you want?

options.text: A quick throw to a hot route
options.why: The ball has to beat the rush; there's no deep help, so a catch can go far.
More rushers than blockers: no time.
Sometimes catches the blitz, but the numbers are against it.

steps.explanation: Against Cover 0, get the ball out.

steps.prompt: After a 25-yard gain, the defense is gassed and trying to substitute. What do you do?

options.text: Go tempo: snap before they can sub
options.why: Tired players and a scrambling defense are an advantage you keep by hurrying.
Fine, but you let them reset.
Gives them the rest they need.

steps.prompt: 1st and 10 at midfield. Your run game is working and they've put eight defenders in the box. What's the call?

options.why: Eight in the box means one-on-one coverage behind defenders who'll bite on the fake.
Can work, but the numbers favor them.
No reason to waste a down.

steps.explanation: When they load the box, play-action punishes it.

steps.prompt: 3rd and 6 at their 12, down 3 with 8:00 left. What's the priority?

options.text: Throw to the sticks or the end zone
options.why: A first down or a touchdown is worth far more than settling now with time left.

options.text: Run to set up the field goal
options.why: Secures three points but likely ends the drive.

options.text: Throw it out of the back of the end zone
options.why: Wastes the down.

steps.explanation: In the red zone with time left, keep the drive alive for seven.

steps.prompt: You lead by 7 with 4:00 left. 3rd and 7 at your 30; they have three timeouts. What's the call?

options.why: A conversion lets you burn more clock and keep the ball.
Safe, but they get the ball back with time and timeouts.
Low-percentage, and an incompletion stops the clock.

steps.explanation: Moving the chains is the best clock management.
